title: Are Americans leaving work, or just getting older?
text:
The share of Americans aged 16 and over who are working or looking for work fell from 66.2 percent in March 1990 to 62.1 percent in March 2026. A four-point fall sounds like a lot of people giving up on work.
The question this post answers is: did participation fall because Americans of a given age became less likely to work, or because more Americans are now at ages when people usually do not work? The first would be a labor-market problem. The second is demographic arithmetic that no labor-market policy can undo.
The national rate is a weighted average of age-group rates,
\[\text{LFP}_t = \sum_a s_{a,t} \, p_{a,t},\]
where \(p_{a,t}\) is participation in age group \(a\) and \(s_{a,t}\) is that group’s share of the adult population. It can fall because the \(p\)’s fall (behavior) or because the \(s\)’s shift toward low-participation groups (composition). The three charts take these in turn: Figure 1 shows the rates, Figure 2 the shares, and Figure 3 recombines them to see which one moved the total.

title: Are Americans leaving work, or just getting older?
text:
The data
Every March Basic Monthly sample from IPUMS CPS, 1990 to 2026, with age, labor-force status and the person weight WTFINL. Every rate and share is weighted:

adults |>
  group_by(year, age_group) |>
  summarise(lfp        = weighted.mean(in_lf, wtfinl),
            population = sum(wtfinl))

The universe is people 16 and over with LABFORCE in (1, 2). Weighting matters here: the unweighted rate for March 2026 is 59.3 percent against a weighted 62.1, because people over 65 are 28.9 percent of the interviewed sample and 23.4 percent of the population. Older people answer the survey more often, which is exactly the group this post is about.

title: Are Americans leaving work, or just getting older?
section: Did behavior change? Participation by age
text:
Did behavior change? Participation by age








Figure 1: The behavior piece: weighted labor-force participation by age group, March of each year. Every group over 25 ends above where it started.





Workers aged 25 to 54 participate at 84.2 percent, against 83.4 percent in 1990. The 55 to 64 group went from 55.6 to 67.2 percent, and participation after 65 rose from 12.2 to 19.1 percent. The one group that pulled back is the youngest, down 11.1 points, probably mostly school enrollment, which this extract cannot confirm. On the behavioral side, then, the answer is no: past age 25, people work more than they did in 1990.

title: Are Americans leaving work, or just getting older?
section: Did the population change? Age shares
text:
Did the population change? Age shares








Figure 2: The composition piece: share of the population aged 16 and over, by age group. The 65+ group, which participates least, gained eight points.





People over 65 were 15.4 percent of the adult population in 1990 and are 23.4 percent now. The prime-age group fell from 55.8 to 47.3 percent. Since participation after 65 is around a fifth and participation between 25 and 54 is above four fifths, that reshuffling pulls the national average down on its own, without anyone changing their mind about work. On the composition side, the answer is yes.

title: Are Americans leaving work, or just getting older?
text:
Which one moved the total?








Figure 3: Putting them together: actual participation and two counterfactuals. The dashed line keeps 1990 age shares (behavior only); the dotted line keeps 1990 rates (aging only).





Freeze the age structure at its 1990 shares and let participation move as it actually did: the rate ends at 67.0 percent, slightly above where it started. Freeze participation instead and let only the age structure move: the rate falls to 60.0 percent. The entire decline in the headline number, and more, is demographics.
The actual line sits above the aging-only line because the groups gaining population share are the ones raising their participation: older Americans working longer has offset about 2.1 points of what aging would otherwise have taken out.

title: Are Americans leaving work, or just getting older?
section: What the three charts say together
text:
What the three charts say together
Figure 1 rules out the behavioral story for everyone over 25. Figure 2 shows the population moving toward the age group with the lowest participation. Figure 3 shows that this shift alone accounts for the whole decline: with the 1990 age mix, participation today would be higher than it was in 1990. Americans are not leaving work; the country is getting older.
Two lessons follow. The headline rate is a poor gauge of labor-market health, because it falls whenever the population ages; the prime-age rate in Figure 1, now 84.2 percent and within 0.3 points of its 2000 peak, is the better signal. And because the youngest baby boomers do not turn 65 until 2029, the headline rate will probably keep drifting down even if every age group keeps working as much as it does now. A falling participation rate in the next few years should not, by itself, be read as Americans giving up on work.

title: Are Americans leaving work, or just getting older?
text:
Caveats
Each point is one March, so 2021 carries the pandemic. Census-based reweighting leaves small breaks around 2000, 2010 and 2020. And a shift-share split is an accounting identity: it locates the change in the age structure but does not explain why 60-year-olds now work more.
Scripts are in R/ and details in README.md; the raw extract stays out of the repository, and 01_acquire.R rebuilds it with an IPUMS account.

title: How much of Philadelphia’s campus poverty is students?
text:
A poverty map of Philadelphia shows the neighborhoods around its three big universities in the same dark shade as Kensington and North Philadelphia. Part of that is real, and part of it is that college students report very little income.
The question: how much of the measured poverty around Philadelphia’s campuses is college students, and how poor are these neighborhoods without them?
The four figures answer this in sequence. Figure 1 is the map as usually drawn. Figure 2 shows where off-campus students live. Figure 3 redraws the first map, same color scale, with students removed. Figure 4 puts each campus tract’s two rates side by side.

title: How much of Philadelphia’s campus poverty is students?
text:
Data
Census tracts from the 2020-2024 American Community Survey 5-year estimates and Census TIGER/Line boundaries, both pulled with tidycensus. Table B14006 reports poverty status separately for undergraduates, graduate students and everyone else, so the split is arithmetic:

pov_all    = pov_poor / pov_universe
pov_noncol = (pov_poor - col_poor) / (pov_universe - col_pop)

Poverty status is not measured for people in dormitories, so only off-campus students enter these numbers. Every map shows rates rather than counts, and tracts with fewer than 500 people in the relevant group are grey. Campus tracts, outlined in black, are tracts within a kilometre of Penn, Drexel or Temple where students make up at least a quarter of residents.

title: How much of Philadelphia’s campus poverty is students?
text:
The map as usually drawn








Figure 1: Poverty rate, all residents, by census tract. Black outlines mark campus tracts; grey tracts have fewer than 500 residents (parks, the airport, industrial land).





Pooled, the campus tracts in University City have a poverty rate of 47.4 percent and those around Temple 52.1 percent, against 20.6 percent in the rest of the city.

title: How much of Philadelphia’s campus poverty is students?
text:
Where students live








Figure 2: Off-campus college and graduate students as a share of residents.





Students cluster in two places, and they are poor on paper: 67 percent of students in the University City campus tracts and 86 percent around Temple fall below the poverty line, because most live on loans and family support that the survey does not count as income.

title: How much of Philadelphia’s campus poverty is students?
section: The same map without students, up close
text:
The same map without students, up close








Figure 3: Central Philadelphia, poverty rate for all residents (left) and for residents who are not college or graduate students (right). Same color scale as the first map; black outlines mark campus tracts, grey marks tracts with too few residents to measure.





Away from the campuses almost nothing changes: the rest of the city goes from 20.6 to 20.4 percent. Around the campuses the dark patches fade without disappearing. Non-student poverty is 30.6 percent in University City and 31.0 percent around Temple.








Figure 4: Each campus tract’s poverty rate with and without students. The dashed line is the non-student poverty rate for the rest of the city. Tract 88.01 has too few non-students to measure.

title: How much of Philadelphia’s campus poverty is students?
section: What the four figures say together
text:
What the four figures say together
Figure 1 overstates campus poverty, and Figure 2 shows why: the dark patches sit exactly where off-campus students live, and students are almost all poor on paper. But Figure 3 shows that removing them does not make the campus neighborhoods ordinary. Students account for between a third and two fifths of the measured rate, and the non-students who remain are about half again as likely to be poor as residents of the rest of the city. Philadelphia’s universities sit in poor neighborhoods; the map makes those neighborhoods look 55 to 68 percent poorer than they are.
Figure 4 adds that this is not uniform. Tract 369.02, on the Center City side of University City, falls to roughly the city average once students are removed, as does tract 153 near Temple. Tract 147, southwest of Temple’s campus, stays above 60 percent.
So both obvious readings of the raw map are wrong. Taking it at face value overstates poverty near campus; dismissing campus-area poverty as “just students” misses that five of the seven measurable campus tracts are still above 20 percent without them. For anyone ranking neighborhoods by need, the correction takes one extra ACS table.

title: How much of Philadelphia’s campus poverty is students?
text:
Caveats
Tract estimates carry wide margins of error, and five-year pooling blends 2020 to 2024, including the pandemic. The one-kilometre and 25 percent thresholds that define a campus tract are judgment calls. And “poor on paper” is not the same as hardship for students, though for their non-student neighbors it usually is.
Scripts are in R/ and details in README.md. Data: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2020-2024 5-year estimates and TIGER/Line cartographic boundary files, accessed 18 October 2026.

title: The average that disagrees with all of its parts
text:
In 1973 the graduate school at Berkeley admitted about 44% of men who applied and about 30% of women. Thousands of applicants sit behind those two numbers, so the gap is not noise. Split the same applicants by department and it very nearly disappears. In the largest department of all, women were admitted at a higher rate than men.
Nothing was recounted. The two statements are about the same people.

title: The average that disagrees with all of its parts
section: What the Berkeley numbers look like
text:
What the Berkeley numbers look like
R ships with the data, so you can check this in four lines.

rates <- as.data.frame(UCBAdmissions) |>
  group_by(Dept, Gender) |>
  summarise(applicants = sum(Freq),
            admitted   = sum(Freq[Admit == "Admitted"]),
            .groups    = "drop") |>
  mutate(rate = admitted / applicants)

rates |>
  select(Dept, Gender, applicants, rate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Gender, values_from = c(applicants, rate)) |>
  transmute(Department    = Dept,
            `Men applied` = applicants_Male,
            `Men admitted` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rate_Male),
            `Women applied` = applicants_Female,
            `Women admitted` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rate_Female)) |>

title: The average that disagrees with all of its parts
text:
Why ratios can do this
A pooled rate is a weighted average of the department rates,
\[
\bar r = \sum_d w_d \, r_d, \qquad w_d = \frac{n_d}{\sum_k n_k},
\]
and the weights \(w_d\) are part of the data, not a constant you can divide out. Men and women faced the same \(r_d\) but carried different \(w_d\), and the difference in weights is bigger than the differences in rates. Pooling therefore measures something nobody intended to measure: where each group chose to apply.

title: The average that disagrees with all of its parts
text:
Why it feels impossible
Counts behave the way intuition expects. If men outnumber women in every department, they outnumber women overall, always. We quietly extend that rule to percentages, and for percentages it is false. Adding a fraction to a fraction means adding numerators and denominators separately, and the denominators are free to move.
The phenomenon predates its name by half a century. Pearson noticed in 1899 that mixing two populations manufactures correlations that exist in neither, and Yule gave the contingency-table version in 1903. Simpson’s 1951 paper worked out what the reversal means for interpreting interaction, and Blyth attached his name to it in 1972. Yule had it first, which is why some writers call it the Yule-Simpson effect.
One thing the Berkeley example does not show is that there was no discrimination. Bickel and his coauthors, writing in Science in 1975, made that point themselves: conditioning on department moves the question rather than closing it, since departments differ in funding and capacity, and applicants do not choose where to apply in a vacuum.

title: The average that disagrees with all of its parts
text:
Takeaway
A pooled comparison is an average, and an average has weights. When two groups are averaged with different weights, the pooled numbers can point the opposite way from every group inside them. Before you read anything into a headline rate, find out what is being averaged and how the weights differ. The reversal is not a rare pathology; it is what happens whenever composition and outcome are related.
Admissions counts are UCBAdmissions in R’s datasets package, from Bickel, Hammel and O’Connell (1975), Science 187, 398–404.

title: Matching parents and children in the PSID with SQL
text: The intergenerational elasticity of income (IGE) is the slope from regressing children’s log income on their parents’ log income. An IGE of 0.4 means a child whose parents earned 10 percent more earns about 4 percent more as an adult. Estimating it requires putting parents’ and children’s income in the same row. This post does that for the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) with SQLite, through Python’s built-in sqlite3 module.

title: Matching parents and children with SQL in Python
section: Step 1: load the panel into SQL
text:
Step 1: load the panel into SQL
The panel has one row per person, identified by a 1968 family ID (ER30001) and a person number (ER30002), with five variables per survey year: interview number, sequence number, relation to the household head, age and family income. A second file gives each person’s mother and father. SQL works best on long tables, so we reshape first:

import sqlite3
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

extract   = pd.read_csv("data/panel/psid_individual_extract.csv")
parent_id = pd.read_csv("data/panel/psid_parent_id.csv")
cpi       = pd.read_csv("data/cpi_annual.csv")

person_year = (pd.wide_to_long(extract, ["intnum", "seqno", "relhead", "age", "faminc"],
                               i=["ER30001", "ER30002"], j="year", sep="_")
                 .reset_index())

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
person_year.to_sql("person_year", con, index=False)
parent_id.to_sql("parent_id", con, index=False)
cpi.to_sql("cpi", con, index=False)

def sql(query):
    return pd.read_sql(query, con)

title: Matching parents and children with SQL in Python
text:
Step 2: SELECT, WHERE and JOIN
SELECT picks and computes columns, WHERE keeps usable rows: people actually in an interviewed family (sequence number 1 to 20), with a known age and positive income. Income in each survey refers to the previous calendar year and is in nominal dollars, so a JOIN to the CPI table converts it to 2022 dollars:

con.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE income AS
SELECT p.ER30001 * 1000 + p.ER30002   AS person_id,
       p.year                         AS survey_year,
       p.age,
       p.relhead,
       p.faminc * base.cpi / c.cpi    AS real_inc
FROM person_year AS p
JOIN cpi AS c    ON c.year = p.year - 1
JOIN cpi AS base ON base.year = 2022
WHERE p.seqno BETWEEN 1 AND 20
  AND p.age < 999
  AND p.faminc > 0;
""")

title: Matching parents and children with SQL in Python
section: Step 3: parents’ income with GROUP BY
text:
Step 3: parents’ income with GROUP BY
Parents are observed from 1983 to 1987, when their children were young. GROUP BY person_id collapses each parent’s five rows into one, and the aggregate functions say how. Because AVG ignores NULL, wrapping it around a CASE averages only the years the condition picks, so one query gives one-year through five-year averages:

con.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE parent_inc AS
SELECT person_id,
       AVG(CASE WHEN survey_year = 1985               THEN real_inc END) AS inc_1yr,
       AVG(CASE WHEN survey_year BETWEEN 1985 AND 1986 THEN real_inc END) AS inc_2yr,
       AVG(CASE WHEN survey_year BETWEEN 1984 AND 1986 THEN real_inc END) AS inc_3yr,
       AVG(CASE WHEN survey_year BETWEEN 1984 AND 1987 THEN real_inc END) AS inc_4yr,
       AVG(real_inc)                                                       AS inc_5yr
FROM income
WHERE survey_year BETWEEN 1983 AND 1987
GROUP BY person_id
HAVING COUNT(*) = 5;
""")

<sqlite3.Cursor at 0x3128422c0>


HAVING filters after grouping; requiring all five years keeps the sample identical across the measures, so any difference in the estimates comes from measurement alone.

title: Matching parents and children with SQL in Python
text:
Step 4: match children to parents
The parent file links each child to a mother and a father. We take the mother where she is identified and the father otherwise, then measure the child’s own income in 2001 to 2023, only in years when they head a household or are the head’s spouse or partner (codes 10, 20, 22), averaged over ages 35 to 45:

con.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE pairs AS
SELECT child_id68 * 1000 + child_pn AS child_id,
       CASE WHEN mother_pn > 0 THEN mother_id68 * 1000 + mother_pn
            ELSE                    father_id68 * 1000 + father_pn END AS parent_id
FROM parent_id
WHERE mother_pn > 0 OR father_pn > 0;

CREATE TABLE child_inc AS
SELECT person_id, AVG(real_inc) AS inc_35_45
FROM income
WHERE survey_year >= 2001 AND relhead IN (10, 20, 22) AND age BETWEEN 35 AND 45
GROUP BY person_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;
""")

sample = sql("""
SELECT pr.child_id, ch.inc_35_45, pa.*
FROM pairs      AS pr
JOIN child_inc  AS ch ON ch.person_id = pr.child_id
JOIN parent_inc AS pa ON pa.person_id = pr.parent_id
""")

An inner JOIN keeps a row only when both sides match, leaving 3,025 parent-child pairs.

title: Matching parents and children with SQL in Python
section: Step 5: one year of income versus several
text:
Step 5: one year of income versus several
The IGE is the OLS slope of log child income on log parent income, estimated once for each parental income measure:

sample["log_child"] = np.log(sample["inc_35_45"])

rows = []
for k in range(1, 6):
    fit = smf.ols(f"log_child ~ np.log(inc_{k}yr)", sample).fit()
    rows.append({"years": k, "ige": fit.params.iloc[1], "se": fit.bse.iloc[1]})
ige = pd.DataFrame(rows)



Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.0))
ax.axhline(0.45, color=GREY, ls="--", lw=1)
ax.text(0.02, 0.457, "true IGE = 0.45", transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(),
        va="bottom", color=GREY, fontsize=9)
ax.errorbar(ige["years"], ige["ige"], yerr=1.96 * ige["se"], fmt="o", color=BLUE, capsize=3)
ax.set_xticks(range(1, 6)); ax.set_xlim(0.6, 5.4); ax.set_ylim(0, 0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("years of parental income averaged"); ax.set_ylabel("estimated IGE")
plt.show()








Figure 1: Estimated IGE by the number of years of parental income averaged, with 95 percent confidence intervals.





One year of parental income gives 0.28; five years give 0.35. A single year mixes permanent income \(\mu\) with a transitory shock \(v\), such as a layoff or a bonus, which acts as measurement error and shrinks the slope:
\[
\hat\beta \;\to\; \beta \cdot \frac{\operatorname{Var}(\mu)}{\operatorname{Var}(\mu) + \operatorname{Var}(\bar v)} .
\]
Averaging shrinks \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar v)\), but less than in proportion to the number of years because shocks persist, so five years still falls short. Solon (1992) made this argument against early US estimates of around 0.2; Mazumder (2005), averaging many more years, put the IGE near 0.6.

title: Matching parents and children with SQL in Python
text:
Step 6: life-cycle bias
People with high lifetime incomes tend to start slowly and then pull ahead, so income measured at 25 compresses differences that are obvious by 45. Re-estimating with the child’s income measured at different ages:

by_age = sql("""
SELECT pr.child_id, i.age, i.real_inc, pa.inc_5yr
FROM pairs      AS pr
JOIN income     AS i  ON i.person_id  = pr.child_id
JOIN parent_inc AS pa ON pa.person_id = pr.parent_id
WHERE i.survey_year >= 2001 AND i.relhead IN (10, 20, 22) AND i.age BETWEEN 25 AND 54
""")
by_age["band"] = pd.cut(by_age["age"], [24, 29, 34, 39, 44, 49, 54],
                        labels=["25-29", "30-34", "35-39", "40-44", "45-49", "50-54"])

rows = []
for band, g in by_age.groupby("band", observed=True):
    per_child = g.groupby("child_id").agg(child=("real_inc", "mean"), parent=("inc_5yr", "first"))
    fit = smf.ols("np.log(child) ~ np.log(parent)", per_child).fit()
    rows.append({"age": band, "ige": fit.params.iloc[1], "se": fit.bse.iloc[1]})
lifecycle = pd.DataFrame(rows)



Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.0))
ax.axhline(0.45, color=GREY, ls="--", lw=1)
ax.text(0.02, 0.457, "true IGE = 0.45", transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(),
        va="bottom", color=GREY, fontsize=9)
x = np.arange(len(lifecycle))
ax.errorbar(x, lifecycle["ige"], yerr=1.96 * lifecycle["se"], fmt="o", color=ORANGE, capsize=3)
ax.set_xticks(x, lifecycle["age"]); ax.set_ylim(0, 0.55)
ax.set_xlabel("child's age when income is measured"); ax.set_ylabel("estimated IGE")
plt.show()








Figure 2: Estimated IGE by the child’s age when income is measured, using the parent’s five-year average.





Measured at 25 to 29 the IGE is 0.26; at 40 to 44 it is 0.36. Haider and Solon (2006) found that current income stops understating lifetime differences around 40. The older bands look closer to 0.45 only because late-career income overstates lifetime differences, offsetting the parental attenuation from Step 5: two biases cancelling, not a better measure.

title: Matching parents and children with SQL in Python
text:
Why averaging in mid-career works
The two biases need different fixes. Averaging several years removes much of the transitory noise in a single year (Figure 1). Measuring around age 40 removes the compression of young adults’ income (Figure 2), which averaging alone cannot do if every year averaged is at 25. The best proxy for long-run economic status is therefore an average over several years, taken in mid-career, for both generations.

title: Paying for wins
text: A team with $30 million of cap space this October can buy about 4.2 points of VORP with it, or about 1.5, depending entirely on which part of the salary market it shops in. VORP is Basketball-Reference’s value over replacement player, and multiplying by 2.7 turns it into wins, so the gap between those two numbers is about 7 wins for the same money.

title: Paying for wins
text:
Getting the data
Basketball-Reference publishes last season’s player statistics and next season’s contracts as ordinary HTML tables. There is no API and no bulk download for them, which is what puts this in scraping territory. Their robots.txt blocks game logs, splits and lineups but leaves /leagues/ and /contracts/ open, and asks for a three second crawl delay, so the acquisition script sends two requests four seconds apart, identifies itself in the user agent, and saves the HTML to disk.

page <- read_html("https://www.basketball-reference.com/leagues/NBA_2026_advanced.html")
xml2::write_html(page, "data/raw/bbref_advanced_2026.html")

advanced <- page |>
  html_element("#advanced") |>
  html_table()

Saving the snapshot matters more than it looks. Every later step parses the local file, so fixing a bug costs zero additional requests, and if the site redesigns its tables next spring the analysis still runs against the page I actually saw.
Two things in the parsed tables would have quietly corrupted the result. Player names carry bracketed footnote markers, so Jokić[a] and Jokić fail to join. And a player traded mid-season gets one row per team plus a combined 2TM row, all sharing a rank, so James Harden appears three times unless the partial rows are dropped. Salaries arrive as strings like $62,587,158, which parse_number() handles.
Because VORP is a fixed function of two other scraped columns, \((\text{BPM} + 2) \times \text{MP} / (48 \times 82)\), recomputing it is a free test of the whole parse. Across 348 players the largest disagreement is rounding, which rules out shifted columns and numbers read as text.

title: Paying for wins
text:
What production costs
Joining production to salary on player name matched 86 percent of contracts. The misses are not spelling errors: they are 2026 draft picks with no NBA minutes and stars who missed all of last season hurt, which is worth remembering when reading anything below about the top of the market.








Figure 1: Total salary divided by total positive VORP, within each salary band. Players with at least 500 minutes in 2025-26, priced against their 2026-27 salary.





Production gets more expensive as salaries rise, which is what competition for scarce talent is supposed to do. The surprise is where the line stops rising. The most expensive production in the league is not at the top: it is in the $15 to $30 million band, at $19.9 million per point, above the $17.3 million that players earning more than $30 million cost.
Two rules explain the shape. At the top, the collective bargaining agreement caps individual salaries, so the best players in the league cannot be paid what they are worth. At the bottom, minimum and rookie scale contracts are set by rule rather than by bidding, and a young player who turns out to be good stays cheap for years. The $15 to $30 million band has neither protection. It is priced by open negotiation for players good enough to be paid but not good enough to be capped, and it is the one place where teams routinely pay full price.

title: Paying for wins
text:
What to do with that
For a team with cap space and no path to a superstar, the advice is to spend at the extremes and stay out of the middle. Four players at $7 million who each produce half a point of VORP return twice what one player at $28 million producing a single point does, for the same money. The limit is the roster: 15 spots and 240 minutes a night, so a team that already has useful cheap players cannot simply buy more of them, and improving a good roster does eventually require paying for production per minute rather than per dollar.
Two caveats. VORP is a box score estimate and misses everything that does not end in a counted event, and the salary is for next season while the production is from last season, which will be wrong about exactly the players who change most.
Both scripts are in R/, the raw HTML snapshots and a provenance record in data/raw/, and the tidy file behind the chart in data/derived/. Only 01_acquire.R touches the network. Data from Basketball-Reference, accessed 20 September 2026.

title: Most of the productivity-pay gap is a unit conversion
text:
Output per hour in the US nonfarm business sector is 159 percent higher than it was in the first quarter of 1973. The average hourly wage of a production worker, deflated by consumer prices, is 3 percent higher. Those two numbers are the usual evidence that workers stopped sharing in what they produce.
Figure 1: Labor productivity and the production worker’s real wage, 1973 Q1 = 100. The series start in 1964, where the wage data begins.
The two lines sit on top of each other until the mid-1970s and then separate, which is where the story usually stops. But productivity and that wage are not measured in the same units, and they do not refer to the same paycheck. Fixing each in turn closes most of the gap.

title: Most of the productivity-pay gap is a unit conversion
text:
The deflator
Productivity is real output: what a sector produces, valued at the prices of the things it produces. The wage above is deflated by the consumer price index, which measures what a paycheck buys. A firm deciding whether an extra hour of labor is worth its cost compares both to the price of its own output, so for that comparison the output deflator is the consistent one.
The two price indices have not moved together. Housing, healthcare and education dominate consumer spending and barely appear in business output prices, while computers and imported goods pull the output deflator down. Swapping the consumer deflator for the output deflator, holding the pay measure fixed, is worth 56 index points.

title: Most of the productivity-pay gap is a unit conversion
text:
The paycheck
AHETPI covers production and nonsupervisory workers, roughly four fifths of private employment, and it counts wages only. Compensation adds employer-paid health insurance and retirement contributions, which is money the employer spends on labor whether or not it shows up in a wage, and it covers everyone including managers. Moving from one to the other is worth 59 points.
This wedge is not purely bookkeeping. Part of it is benefits, and part of it is that pay growth went to people above the production and nonsupervisory line. These series cannot separate the two, and the second part is a real distributional change rather than a measurement choice.








Figure 2: The same gap, with each transformation added in turn. Each step up is one change of units or one change of pay concept.





What survives both corrections is the distance between productivity and real compensation measured in the same prices: 42 points, or 27 percent of the original gap. That residual is labor’s share of output, and it is the only piece that means what the headline chart is usually taken to mean.

title: Most of the productivity-pay gap is a unit conversion
text:
When each piece opened








Figure 3: The gap in Figure 1, split into three. The three lines add to the total at every date.





The three pieces arrived in order. The pay-concept wedge opened first, in the late 1970s, and had done most of its work by 2000 as employer health costs grew. The deflator wedge has widened at a near-constant rate since the early 1980s. The labor-share wedge, the one that actually describes workers getting a smaller slice, sat near zero for the first thirty years and only crossed ten points in 2005. It is now 42.
So the common summary, that pay stopped tracking productivity in the early 1970s, is pointing at the right chart and the wrong decade. Labor’s share of what it produced held up through the 1980s and 1990s. It started falling around 2000, which is a narrower claim, a more recent one, and a more useful one if the question is what changed.

title: Most of the productivity-pay gap is a unit conversion
text:
Caveats
Compensation here is an average, so it is pulled up by pay at the top; the distance between average compensation and what a median worker earns is inequality rather than measurement, and it is sitting inside the pay-concept wedge. Productivity is gross of depreciation, and a net measure would close a few more points, since capital wears out faster than it used to. The 1973 base quarter is a convention rather than a fact about the data.
Both scripts are in R/, with the series list and the construction in README.md. Data from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, accessed 6 October 2026.

title: Matching parents and children in the PSID with SQL
text:
The intergenerational elasticity of income, or IGE, is the slope from regressing children’s log income on their parents’ log income. An IGE of 0.4 means a child whose parents earned 10 percent more earns about 4 percent more as an adult. Estimating it needs the parents’ income and the child’s income in the same row, and no survey file comes that way. This post builds those rows from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) with SQL run from Python, estimates the IGE, and then shows how much the estimate depends on how many years of income go into it and on the ages at which income is measured.
All the SQL runs in SQLite through Python’s built-in sqlite3 module, so there is no database server to install.

title: Matching parents and children in the PSID with SQL
text:
The data
The PSID has interviewed the members of about 5,000 US families since 1968, and it keeps following their children after they leave home and start households of their own. That rule is what makes parent-child matching possible: a grown child of a PSID family is interviewed as a PSID family in their own right. Three downloads from the PSID website are used here.

The cross-year individual file, ind2023er, has one row per person ever in the study. A person is identified by the 1968 interview number of their original family (ER30001) and a person number within it (ER30002). For every wave it records the interview number of the family the person lived in, their sequence number in that family, their relationship to the reference person, and their age.
The Parent Identification File, pid23, gives each person’s birth mother and birth father, each as a (1968 interview number, person number) pair.
A family-file extract from the PSID Data Center with the labor income of the reference person and of the spouse or partner in the 2017, 2019, 2021 and 2023 waves. The PSID has interviewed every other year since 1997, and income questions refer to the previous calendar year, so these are incomes for 2016, 2018, 2020 and 2022.

The individual file is a 560 MB fixed-width text file. The script py/01_prepare.py reads only the columns used below, taking their positions from the Stata .do file that comes with the download, and writes three small CSV files. The PSID does not allow its data to be redistributed, so neither the downloads nor the CSV files are in this site’s repository; the README for this post says how to rebuild them.

Step 1: load the tables into SQLite
The individual file is wide, with one row per person and four columns per wave. Joins are much simpler on long tables, so pd.wide_to_long turns it into one row per person per wave before it goes into the database.

import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

cpi         = pd.read_csv("data/cpi_annual.csv")

                               i=["id68", "pn"], j="survey_year", sep="_")
                 .reset_index())

person_year.to_sql("person_year", con, index=False)

section: Step 2: attach family income to people with JOIN
text:
Step 2: attach family income to people with JOIN
The family extract needs care. In a Data Center extract that contains only family-file variables, the columns for the four waves sit side by side, but a row is not the same family across waves: row 5 of the 2017 columns and row 5 of the 2019 columns are unrelated households. 01_prepare.py therefore cut each wave out on its own, so family_income has one row per family per wave, keyed by survey_year and family_id, the interview number. An interview number identifies a family only within a wave.
The link between waves runs through people. The individual file stores, for every person and wave, the interview number of the family they lived in, so a JOIN on both the survey year and the interview number attaches each person to their family’s income that wave.

run("""
CREATE TABLE income AS
SELECT p.id68 * 1000 + p.pn                     AS person_id,
       p.survey_year - 1                        AS inc_year,
       p.age - 1                                AS age,
       p.rel,
       (f.rp_labor + f.sp_labor) * base.cpi / c.cpi AS fam_labor
FROM person_year AS p
JOIN family_income AS f
  ON f.survey_year = p.survey_year AND f.family_id = p.intnum
JOIN cpi AS c    ON c.year = p.survey_year - 1
JOIN cpi AS base ON base.year = 2022
WHERE (p.rel = 10 AND p.seqno = 1)
   OR (p.rel IN (20, 22) AND p.seqno BETWEEN 1 AND 20);
""")

The income measure is family labor income: the reference person’s labor income plus the spouse’s. Measuring both generations at the family level is the usual choice in this literature, and it puts married and single people on the same footing as far as the data allow. PSID labor income here is wages, salaries, bonuses, overtime, tips, commissions and professional practice income; it excludes farm income and the labor part of business income.

text:
Step 3: link children to parents
The Parent Identification File has one row per person with up to two parents. Turning it into a long table of (child, parent) links makes the next join straightforward. UNION ALL stacks the results of two SELECT statements with the same columns, one for mothers and one for fathers, and the WHERE clauses drop parents who are not identified (person number 0).

run("""
CREATE TABLE links AS
SELECT id68 * 1000 + pn                 AS child_id,
       mother_id68 * 1000 + mother_pn   AS parent_id,
       'mother'                         AS parent
FROM parents WHERE mother_pn > 0
UNION ALL
SELECT id68 * 1000 + pn,
       father_id68 * 1000 + father_pn,
       'father'
FROM parents WHERE father_pn > 0;
""")

title: Matching parents and children in the PSID with SQL
section: Step 4: one row per child for each generation
text:
Step 4: one row per child for each generation
Both generations’ incomes now sit in the same income table: a child’s own rows, and the rows of the people that links names as that child’s parents. Collapsing them to one row per child takes GROUP BY and aggregation in two stages.
The first stage joins each child to their parents’ income rows and averages over the two parents within each year. If the parents live together, both rows carry the same family income and the average is that number; if they live apart, it is the mean of the two households.

run("""
CREATE TABLE parent_year AS
SELECT l.child_id,
       i.inc_year,
       AVG(i.fam_labor) AS inc,
       AVG(i.age)       AS age
FROM links AS l
JOIN income AS i ON i.person_id = l.parent_id
GROUP BY l.child_id, i.inc_year;
""")

The second stage turns each child’s (up to) four parent-years into one row. Wrapping an aggregate around a CASE expression picks out a single year: CASE returns NULL in the other years, and aggregate functions skip NULLs. HAVING is a WHERE that runs after grouping, so it can filter on aggregates. Here it keeps only children whose parents have positive family labor income in all four years, which keeps the sample fixed across every income measure compared below.

run("""
CREATE TABLE parent_inc AS
SELECT child_id,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2016 THEN inc END) AS p2016,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2018 THEN inc END) AS p2018,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2020 THEN inc END) AS p2020,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2022 THEN inc END) AS p2022,
       AVG(inc)                                    AS p_avg,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2016 THEN age END) AS p_age16
FROM parent_year
GROUP BY child_id
HAVING COUNT(*) = 4 AND MIN(inc) > 0;

CREATE TABLE child_inc AS
SELECT person_id                                         AS child_id,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2016 THEN fam_labor END) AS c2016,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2018 THEN fam_labor END) AS c2018,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2020 THEN fam_labor END) AS c2020,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2022 THEN fam_labor END) AS c2022,
       AVG(fam_labor)                                    AS c_avg,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2016 THEN age END)       AS c_age16
FROM income
GROUP BY person_id
HAVING COUNT(*) = 4 AND MIN(fam_labor) > 0;
""")

child_inc is built from every person in income, not only from people with identified parents. The match in the next step decides who counts as a child.

title: Matching parents and children in the PSID with SQL
section: Step 6: one year of income versus several
text:
Step 6: one year of income versus several
The IGE is the OLS slope of log child income on log parent income.

def ige(df, child, parent):
    """Slope of log(child) on log(parent), SEs clustered on the 1968 family."""
    d = pd.DataFrame({"y": np.log(df[child]), "x": np.log(df[parent]),
                      "g": df["family68"]})
    fit = smf.ols("y ~ x", d).fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": d["g"]})
    return fit.params["x"], fit.bse["x"]

years = [2016, 2018, 2020, 2022]
rows = []
for k in range(1, 5):
    for combo in combinations(years, k):
        s = sample.copy()
        s["p_k"] = s[[f"p{y}" for y in combo]].mean(axis=1)
        s["c_k"] = s[[f"c{y}" for y in combo]].mean(axis=1)
        rows.append({"k": k, "years": combo,
                     "both":         ige(s, "c_k", "p_k")[0],
                     "parents_only": ige(s, "c_avg", "p_k")[0]})
combos = pd.DataFrame(rows)
by_k = combos.groupby("k")[["both", "parents_only"]].mean()

Figure 1: Estimated IGE by the number of years of income averaged. Small dots are individual sets of years; large dots are their mean. Same sample of pairs throughout.





With one year of income for both generations the IGE averages 0.10. Averaging all four years raises it to 0.15, an increase of 51 percent on the same families.
The reason is measurement error. A single year’s income is a family’s long-run income plus a transitory part: a layoff, a bonus, a spell of part-time work, a year off with a new baby. Write log parent income in year \(t\) as \(x_t = x^* + v_t\), with \(x^*\) long-run income and \(v_t\) the transitory part. Regressing child income on \(x_t\) instead of \(x^*\) gives
\[
\operatorname{plim}\hat\beta = \beta \cdot \frac{\operatorname{Var}(x^*)}{\operatorname{Var}(x^*) + \operatorname{Var}(v_t)},
\]
which is smaller than \(\beta\) whenever \(\operatorname{Var}(v_t) > 0\). Averaging over \(T\) years replaces \(v_t\) with \(\bar v\), whose variance is smaller, so the ratio moves toward 1. The data show the transitory part is large. The variance of a single year’s log parental income is 1.25; the variance of the log four-year average is 0.80. The correlation of log parental income between survey years two years apart is 0.73, and between 2016 and 2022 it falls to 0.53. If the gap between single-year income and long-run income were small, those correlations would be close to 1.
Which side gets averaged matters. Measurement error in the regressor (parental income) biases the slope toward zero; classical measurement error in the dependent variable (child income) only adds noise. The orange line holds the child’s measure fixed and averages only the parents: one year of parental income gives 0.10, four years give 0.15. Going the other way, regressing a single year of child income on the parents’ four-year average gives 0.15 on average across the four years, about the same as using the child’s four-year average. Most of the gain from averaging comes from the parental side. Solon (1992) made this point against early US estimates of about 0.2 that used one year of fathers’ earnings; with a five-year average of fathers’ earnings in the PSID he found an IGE of about 0.4.
Even four years is too short to remove all the transitory variation, because transitory shocks persist from one year to the next. Mazumder (2005), using up to 16 years of fathers’ earnings from Social Security records, put the IGE close to 0.6.

title: Matching parents and children in the PSID with SQL
text:
Step 7: life-cycle bias
Averaging addresses noise around long-run income. Life-cycle bias is a different problem: income at a given age can be a systematically distorted picture of lifetime income. People with high lifetime incomes tend to have steep earnings profiles. They earn little in their twenties, often because they are still in school or in junior jobs, and pull ahead in their thirties and forties. Income measured early in a career therefore compresses lifetime differences. Near the end of a career the problem reverses in a different way, as people retire, cut hours or move to part-time jobs at different ages for reasons that have little to do with their lifetime income.
Because the PSID follows the same people over time, the matched sample can show this without changing who is in it. The left panel below holds the parental measure fixed at the four-year average and moves the year in which the child’s income is measured, so the only thing changing is the child’s age. The right panel does the reverse.

title: Matching parents and children in the PSID with SQL
section: Why averaging works, and what it cannot fix
text:
Why averaging works, and what it cannot fix
The two problems call for different fixes. Transitory shocks are roughly independent of long-run income and partly cancel when several years are added up, so the average of \(T\) years tracks long-run income more closely than any single year. That is why the blue and orange lines in Figure 1 rise with the number of years. The gain is smaller than \(1/T\) would suggest, because shocks persist: a layoff in 2018 often still shows in 2020.
Averaging does nothing for life-cycle bias if every year in the average comes from the wrong part of the life cycle. The four-year average for a 26-year-old is an average of four compressed observations, and the average for a 64-year-old is an average of four years around retirement. The best measure of long-run economic status is an average over several years taken when both generations are in mid-career, roughly ages 30 to 50. With PSID data, that means pulling parental income from the waves when the children were growing up, many years before the children’s own income is measured.
That is also why every estimate in this post is well below the 0.4 to 0.6 range in the literature. The extract covers only 2016 to 2022 for both generations, so the parents are measured near the end of their careers and the children near the start, and four survey years is a short window. Two further choices push the estimates down: the sample is limited to children who head their own households in all four waves, and families with zero labor income in any year are dropped because the log of zero is undefined. The estimates are also unweighted, so they describe the PSID sample rather than the US population. The SQL does not need to change to fix the first problem. Adding earlier waves of family income to the Data Center extract, and extending the CASE columns in parent_inc to those years, lets the same pipeline measure parents in their thirties and forties.

Step 2: attach family income to people with JOIN
The family extract needs care. In a Data Center extract that contains only family-file variables, the columns for the four waves sit side by side, but a row is not the same family across waves: row 5 of the 2017 columns and row 5 of the 2019 columns are unrelated households. 01_prepare.py therefore cut each wave out on its own, so family_income has one row per family per wave, keyed by survey_year and family_id, the interview number. An interview number identifies a family only within a wave.
The link between waves runs through people. The individual file stores, for every person and wave, the interview number of the family they lived in, so a JOIN on both the survey year and the interview number attaches each person to their family’s income that wave.

SELECT p.id68 * 1000 + p.pn                     AS person_id,
       p.survey_year - 1                        AS inc_year,

JOIN cpi AS c    ON c.year = p.survey_year - 1
JOIN cpi AS base ON base.year = 2022
WHERE (p.rel = 10 AND p.seqno = 1)

       'father'
FROM parents WHERE father_pn > 0;

section: Step 4: one row per child for each generation
text:
Step 4: one row per child for each generation
Both generations’ incomes now sit in the same income table: a child’s own rows, and the rows of the people that links names as that child’s parents. Collapsing them to one row per child takes GROUP BY and aggregation in two stages.
The first stage joins each child to their parents’ income rows and averages over the two parents within each year. If the parents live together, both rows carry the same family income and the average is that number; if they live apart, it is the mean of the two households.

run("""
CREATE TABLE parent_year AS
SELECT l.child_id,
       i.inc_year,
       AVG(i.fam_labor) AS inc,
       AVG(i.age)       AS age
FROM links AS l
JOIN income AS i ON i.person_id = l.parent_id
GROUP BY l.child_id, i.inc_year;
""")

The second stage turns each child’s (up to) four parent-years into one row. Wrapping an aggregate around a CASE expression picks out a single year: CASE returns NULL in the other years, and aggregate functions skip NULLs. HAVING is a WHERE that runs after grouping, so it can filter on aggregates. Here it keeps only children whose parents have positive family labor income in all four years, which keeps the sample fixed across every income measure compared below.

run("""
CREATE TABLE parent_inc AS
SELECT child_id,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2016 THEN inc END) AS p2016,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2018 THEN inc END) AS p2018,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2020 THEN inc END) AS p2020,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2022 THEN inc END) AS p2022,
       AVG(inc)                                    AS p_avg,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2016 THEN age END) AS p_age16
FROM parent_year
GROUP BY child_id
HAVING COUNT(*) = 4 AND MIN(inc) > 0;

CREATE TABLE child_inc AS
SELECT person_id                                         AS child_id,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2016 THEN fam_labor END) AS c2016,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2018 THEN fam_labor END) AS c2018,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2020 THEN fam_labor END) AS c2020,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2022 THEN fam_labor END) AS c2022,
       AVG(fam_labor)                                    AS c_avg,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2016 THEN age END)       AS c_age16
FROM income
GROUP BY person_id
HAVING COUNT(*) = 4 AND MIN(fam_labor) > 0;
""")

child_inc is built from every person in income, not only from people with identified parents. The match in the next step decides who counts as a child.

def ige(df, child, parent):
    d = pd.DataFrame({"y": np.log(df[child]), "x": np.log(df[parent]), "g": df.family68})
    fit = smf.ols("y ~ x", d).fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": d.g})

One year of income gives an IGE of 0.10; the four-year average gives 0.15. A single year is long-run income \(x^*\) plus a transitory shock \(v_t\) (a layoff, a bonus, a year of part-time work). Using \(x_t = x^* + v_t\) as the regressor gives
\[
\operatorname{plim}\hat\beta = \beta \cdot \frac{\operatorname{Var}(x^*)}{\operatorname{Var}(x^*) + \operatorname{Var}(v_t)} < \beta .
\]
Averaging over several years shrinks the variance of the shock and moves the ratio toward 1. The shocks here are large: log parental income in 2016 and 2022 correlates at only 0.53. The two lines in Figure 1 nearly coincide, so the gain comes from averaging the parents’ income. Error in the child’s income, the dependent variable, adds noise but no bias.

People with high lifetime incomes tend to start slowly and pull ahead in their thirties and forties, so income measured early in a career compresses lifetime differences. Late in a career, retirement and cuts in hours distort it again. Holding the sample fixed, we can move the year in which one generation’s income is measured:

        (axes[1], parent_path, ORANGE, sample.p_age16.mean(), "parents' income in one year")]:

    ax.set_xticks(years, [f"{y}\nage {base + y - 2016:.0f}" for y in years])

run("""
CREATE TABLE income AS
SELECT p.id68 * 1000 + p.pn                         AS person_id,
       p.survey_year - 1                            AS inc_year,
       p.age - 1                                    AS age,
       (f.rp_labor + f.sp_labor) * base.cpi / c.cpi AS fam_labor
FROM person_year AS p
JOIN family_income AS f ON f.survey_year = p.survey_year AND f.family_id = p.intnum
JOIN cpi AS c    ON c.year = p.survey_year - 1
JOIN cpi AS base ON base.year = 2022
WHERE (p.rel = 10 AND p.seqno = 1)                      -- reference person
   OR (p.rel IN (20, 22) AND p.seqno BETWEEN 1 AND 20); -- spouse or partner
""")

title: Matching parents and children in the PSID with SQL
section: Step 3: link children to parents (UNION ALL)
text:
Step 3: link children to parents (UNION ALL)
The parent file has mother and father in separate columns. UNION ALL stacks two SELECTs into one long table of (child, parent) links.

run("""
CREATE TABLE links AS
SELECT id68 * 1000 + pn AS child_id, mother_id68 * 1000 + mother_pn AS parent_id
FROM parents WHERE mother_pn > 0
UNION ALL
SELECT id68 * 1000 + pn, father_id68 * 1000 + father_pn
FROM parents WHERE father_pn > 0;
""")

title: Matching parents and children in the PSID with SQL
section: Step 4: one row per child for each generation (GROUP BY)
text:
Step 4: one row per child for each generation (GROUP BY)
Parents and children both live in income; links says who is whose parent. GROUP BY with aggregate functions collapses rows in two stages. First, average the two parents’ income in each year (the same number if they live together):

run("""
CREATE TABLE parent_year AS
SELECT l.child_id, i.inc_year, AVG(i.fam_labor) AS inc, AVG(i.age) AS age
FROM links AS l JOIN income AS i ON i.person_id = l.parent_id
GROUP BY l.child_id, i.inc_year;
""")

Second, turn each person’s four years into one row. CASE returns NULL outside the chosen year and aggregates skip NULLs, so MAX(CASE ...) picks one year. HAVING filters after grouping: it keeps people with positive income in all four years, so every comparison below uses the same sample.

cols = lambda v: ",\n".join(
    f"MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = {y} THEN {v} END) AS y{y}" for y in (2016, 2018, 2020, 2022))
run(f"""
CREATE TABLE parent_inc AS
SELECT child_id, {cols('inc')}, AVG(inc) AS y_avg,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2016 THEN age END) AS age16
FROM parent_year GROUP BY child_id
HAVING COUNT(*) = 4 AND MIN(inc) > 0;

CREATE TABLE child_inc AS
SELECT person_id AS child_id, {cols('fam_labor')}, AVG(fam_labor) AS y_avg,
       MAX(CASE WHEN inc_year = 2016 THEN age END) AS age16
FROM income GROUP BY person_id
HAVING COUNT(*) = 4 AND MIN(fam_labor) > 0;
""")

title: Matching parents and children in the PSID with SQL
section: Why averaging helps, and its limits
text:
Why averaging helps, and its limits
Transitory shocks are mostly unrelated to long-run income, so they partly cancel in an average, and a multi-year average is closer to long-run status than any single year. Solon (1992) showed that earlier US estimates of about 0.2 were biased down this way and found about 0.4 with five-year averages in the PSID; Mazumder (2005), averaging up to 16 years, found about 0.6. Averaging cannot fix life-cycle bias if every year comes from the wrong age, so the best measure averages several years in mid-career for both generations.
That explains why the estimates here are well below the literature: this extract measures parents late in their careers and children early in their careers, over only four survey years. Adding earlier family-file waves to the extract would let the same SQL measure parents while their children were growing up.
